title: The arginase-polyamine signaling axis in immune cells: Implications for immune modulation and host-pathogen interactions

sections.abstract: The immune system employs complex metabolic pathways to regulate host-pathogen interactions. Among these, the arginase-polyamine axis is a crucial modulator of both innate and adaptive immunity. Despite significant progress, the precise roles and regulatory mechanisms governing the arginase-polyamine axis in immune cell function remain incompletely understood. This review aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the arginase-polyamine axis, highlighting its role in maintaining immune homeostasis and preserving the functional integrity of various immune cell types. Furthermore, we discuss the strategies used by diverse pathogens to manipulate this pathway, facilitating the creation of immunosuppressive microenvironments that promote their intracellular survival and replication in the host. Finally, we highlight the potential of innovative therapeutic strategies that target arginase-polyamine signaling pathways, which can effectively modulate immune responses in the context of infectious diseases.
sections.introduction:
The intricate interplay between the immune system and invading microorganisms is central to maintaining organismal health. This host-pathogen dynamic relies on a sophisticated network of innate and adaptive immune responses, each characterized by specialized mechanisms designed to counteract infectious agents. The innate arm of the immune system includes cells such as macrophages, neutrophils, Natural Killer (NK), γδ T, and other innate T cells, that provide immediate, non-specific defense. In contrast, the adaptive arm, which comprises T and B lymphocytes, provides a precise and long-lasting response. Recent investigations have highlighted the pivotal role of metabolic pathways in modulating immune responses. Among these metabolic pathways, the arginase-polyamine axis has emerged as an important factor in determining immune responses, significantly affecting both innate and adaptive immunity. This axis involves the interaction between arginine metabolism and polyamine biosynthesis, which is essential for maintaining immune cell function and mounting effective host defense against intracellular pathogens.

L-arginine can act as a regulator of immune responses. It serves as a substrate for various enzymatic pathways that produce a range of bioactive molecules, such as nitric oxide (NO), ornithine, proline, creatine, agmatine, and polyamines. 1 Two enzymes primarily govern L-arginine metabolism: nitric oxide synthase (NOS) and arginase (ARG) ( Figure 1 ). NOS catalyzes the conversion of L-arginine to nitric oxide (NO) ( Figure 1 ), which is crucial for clearing intracellular pathogens and activating T-helper 1 (Th1)-type immune responses. In contrast, ARG hydrolyses L-arginine into ornithine and urea ( Figure 1 ), leading to the production of polyamines, which are vital for regulating cell proliferation, gene expression, signal transduction, and immune cell function. 2 The delicate balance between NO and polyamines influences the polarization of immune cells to either pro-inflammatory or anti-inflammatory phenotypes. This equilibrium is crucial for infection control, immune regulation, and tissue homeostasis. Several pathogens are capable of manipulating the arginase-polyamine axis to subvert host immune responses and promote their survival. In this review, we discuss the roles of arginase and polyamines in the regulation of various immune cell types. Furthermore, we describe the strategies employed by various pathogens to manipulate the arginase-polyamine signaling axis to evade host defences. Finally, we discuss the therapeutic potential of targeting the arginase-polyamine pathway. Figure 1 Regulation of L-arginine metabolism by iNOS and arginase in macrophages L-arginine is imported into macrophages from extracellular spaces through the SL7CA1 (Solute carrier family seven members 1) transporter and SLCA2. It serves as a common substrate for both iNOS and Arginase, which can compete with each other and can counter-regulate each other’s activity. Pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IFN-α, IFN-β, and IFN-γ, and so forth activate iNOS, while anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-10 and TGF-β regulate arginase expression. Arginase metabolizes L-arginine into ornithine and urea. Cytosolic ornithine is converted into polyamines, mainly putrescine, spermidine, and spermine, through the sequential actions of ornithine decarboxylase (ODC), spermidine synthase (SRM), and spermine synthase (SMS). Alternatively, Ornithine can also be metabolized by ornithine aminotransferase (OAT) to L-proline, which helps in collagen synthesis. Collectively, these pathways support anti-inflammatory responses, tissue repair, wound healing, and M2 or alternate activation of macrophages. In contrast, iNOS metabolizes L-arginine to produce nitric oxide (NO·) and L-citrulline. NO· in the presence of NADPH can react with superoxide (O2 − ) and molecular oxygen (O 2 ) to form reactive nitrogen species (RNS), including peroxynitrite (ONOO − ), nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ), nitrite (NO2 − ), nitrate (NO3 − ), and dinitrogen trioxide (N 2 O 3 ). These reactive intermediates exert antimicrobial activity by inducing oxidative stress, DNA damage, lipid peroxidation, and M1-type macrophage activation.

sections.conclusion:
The arginase-polyamine axis has emerged as a pivotal metabolic checkpoint that regulates innate and adaptive immunity, with profound implications in infection biology, inflammation, and immune homeostasis. Extensive evidence has demonstrated that both host and pathogen arginases shape the immune microenvironment by modulating L-arginine bioavailability, nitric oxide synthesis, and polyamine production. This dual role provides opportunities for therapeutic targeting, but also presents significant translational challenges, as inhibition strategies must balance the restoration of host immunity with the avoidance of metabolic toxicity or unintended enhancement of pathogen fitness. Over the past century, arginase inhibition has progressed from early α-amino acid inhibitors to rationally designed high-affinity compounds, such as nor-NOHA and boronic acid derivatives. However, persistent hurdles remain, including isoform non-selectivity, poor pharmacokinetics and an incomplete understanding of ARG1/ARG2 cell-specific and temporal regulation in complex immune networks.

Future research should prioritize the development of isoform-specific inhibitors, informed by high-resolution structural and dynamic studies, to dissect the distinct physiological and pathological roles of ARG1 and ARG2. Advanced delivery systems, such as nanoparticle-mediated targeting and pro-drug designs, can improve tissue specificity and therapeutic indices. Complementary strategies, such as monoclonal antibodies with extracellular specificities, RNA interference approaches, and selective targeting of pathogen arginases, hold promise but require optimization for in vivo stability, immune compatibility, and delivery.

Integrating spatial metabolomics, single-cell proteomics, and inducible gene-editing models will refine our understanding of the arginase-polyamine network within tissue-specific immune landscapes. Ultimately, translating these insights into precision immunometabolic interventions will depend on robust pre-clinical validation, biomarker-guided patient selection, and well-designed clinical trials that capture both therapeutic benefits and safety in diverse infectious and inflammatory contexts.
